title: Visitor
objectives: Add a new operation without editing every existing part class.
Trace compile-time overload selection and runtime virtual dispatch.
Choose Visitor only when its type-set tradeoff fits the program.

sections.heading: The problem: the parts stay familiar while reports multiply
paragraphs: A workshop order contains two kinds of item: a group of bolts counted by pieces, and a cable measured in whole metres. Each quantity must be between zero and one hundred. A price report charges five cents per bolt and forty cents per metre. The total cannot exceed one million cents. Direct price methods on Bolts and Cable are a reasonable first design when price is the one operation every item must offer. The next requests are labels, packing summaries, and audit reports, each with different output needs.

Adding every report as another virtual member makes stable data types change whenever a reporting team needs a new operation. A large switch on a type code moves the work outside the classes but loses compiler-checked access to the distinct data of each kind. We need to let an outside operation receive the exact kind of part while callers still traverse a mixed list through the common Part interface. The Visitor pattern provides this connection, at a cost: the set of element types becomes explicit in the visitor interface.
sections.code:
const int bolt_cost = bolts.count() * 5;
const int cable_cost = cable.metres() * 40;

sections.heading: One visitor operation has one entry point for each kind
paragraphs: Visitor declares two overloaded visit functions: one taking const Bolts& and one taking const Cable&. Overloading means several functions share a name but have different parameter lists. Price implements both. It keeps a running cents_ total and uses the correct unit for each kind. Bolts exposes a count getter; Cable exposes a metres getter. Neither class needs to know the price rules or the output format of a future label report.

Part declares accept(Visitor&) const. Each concrete element implements accept and calls visitor.visit with a reference to itself. The const qualifier at the end means this accepting operation cannot change the element through its ordinary members. The visitor reference is not const, because a report visitor may update its own running result. A read-only element and a changing report are compatible: const applies to a particular object and access path, not to the entire call tree.

sections.heading: Why a single overloaded call is not enough
paragraphs: Imagine a Part& variable that actually refers to a Bolts object. Calling visitor.visit(part) cannot select visit(const Bolts&) merely because the runtime object happens to be bolts. Overload resolution, the choice among same-name functions, uses the expression’s static type during compilation. Here the static type is Part&, and Visitor does not offer a Part overload. A downcast at every caller would move type-checking knowledge into all loops, defeating the goal of a common traversal.

Instead the loop calls part->accept(price). Virtual dispatch chooses Bolts::accept during execution because the actual element is Bolts. Inside that member, *this has the type const Bolts, so the compiler selects visit(const Bolts&) when compiling that function. Calling the selected virtual visit then dispatches to the implementation belonging to the actual visitor object, Price. The behavior depends on both the element kind and visitor kind. This two-stage selection is called double dispatch. It combines static overload choice with virtual calls; it does not make ordinary C++ overload resolution dynamic.

sections.heading: Follow ownership without giving it to the visitor
paragraphs: The parts vector owns unique_ptr<Part> values whose actual objects are Bolts and Cable. Part has a virtual destructor so destroying an owning base pointer properly destroys the complete concrete object. Price is a separate local object in main. During accept it borrows each part through a const reference. It does not retain those references, own the parts, or change their quantities. After traversal, the visitor owns only its numeric result.

The forward declarations class Bolts and class Cable tell the compiler that those type names exist before Visitor uses references to them. A reference declaration does not need the complete class layout. The later class definitions provide constructors, getters, and accept bodies. This arrangement resolves the header dependency between the visitor interface and its element types. In a multi-file program, separate headers and forward declarations keep that dependency controlled; putting every implementation in one header can make every report change trigger broad recompilation.

sections.heading: The price calculation also needs ordinary correctness
paragraphs: Design structure does not make arithmetic automatically safe. Constructors reject negative quantities and quantities above one hundred. Each price term is therefore bounded before multiplication: at most five hundred cents for bolts or four thousand cents for cable. Price::add checks whether the accumulated total exceeds one million minus the next nonnegative term. Only then does it add. Checking before addition avoids computing an overflowed result and trying to diagnose it afterward. The chosen limits fit the required int range on the documented compiler platform.

The sample order contains three bolts and two metres of cable. The terms are fifteen and eighty, so the result is ninety-five cents. A fresh visitor starts at zero; a zero-quantity element changes nothing. For the limit test, two hundred fifty visits to a one-hundred-metre cable reach exactly one million. The next visit throws and leaves the old total intact. The visitor therefore has its own invariant and failure policy, separate from those of the elements. Reusing the same Price visitor for another order would accumulate into the previous result unless the caller deliberately creates a new visitor.

sections.heading: Choose which direction of change should be easy
paragraphs: Adding Labels in the lab changes no Bolts, Cable, or Part class. Labels implements both visits and appends strings with quantities and unit names. The same traversal works. However, adding a new element kind such as Paint requires a new visit overload in the Visitor interface and an implementation in every concrete visitor. This can be useful: the compiler forces every operation to decide how to handle Paint. It can also be costly when new element kinds arrive frequently and the operation set barely changes.

C++17 offers another option for a closed set of types: std::variant<BoltsData, CableData> can store exactly one alternative, and std::visit selects a callable for the active alternative. This can avoid a heap allocation and a virtual base hierarchy for simple value data. It still makes the type set explicit, and visitors must handle its alternatives. Ordinary virtual members remain simpler when new types are common and the operation set is stable. Visitor is a tradeoff between these directions of change, not a general rule to move every method out of its class.

example.title: Price a mixed workshop order
requirements: Support bolt counts and cable lengths with distinct units.
Compute exact integer-cent totals with a one-million-cent limit.
Keep reporting operations outside stable part data classes.
example.design: Each Part accepts a Visitor, and each concrete part forwards its own precise type. Price implements the type-specific operations and retains a checked running total.
example.alternative: Virtual price members are simpler if price is intrinsic and the operation set is stable. A variant and std::visit suit a closed set of simple value types. Visitor is useful when adding operations across stable element types is the main change.
invariants: Each part quantity is in 0 through 100.
Price is between zero and one million cents.
A visitor reads parts without taking ownership.
Every concrete visitor supplies an operation for every declared element kind.

failures.mistake: Call visit directly with a Part reference and expect the Bolts overload to be chosen dynamically.
failures.consequence: The call does not compile with this interface because neither concrete-reference overload accepts a Part reference.
failures.reason: Overload resolution uses the static expression type; accept supplies the missing concrete-type step.

failures.mistake: Reuse one Price object for two independent identical orders without resetting it.
failures.consequence: The second displayed total becomes 190 instead of 95.
failures.reason: The visitor retains a running total across visits.

example.verification: The executable checks a mixed order total, a fresh empty result, zero quantity, rejected negative cable length, exact price limit, and rejection above the limit without mutation. The code guards upper quantity bounds, but the primary tests do not enumerate every constructor bound.
example.maintenance: A new report becomes a visitor with an explicit case for every type. A new type becomes a deliberate cross-operation change; use compiler errors and tests to locate all affected report behavior.

diagram.title: Visitor: outside operations on stable element kinds
diagram.explanation: Inheritance arrows point from concrete classes toward their bases. Dependency arrows show parameter knowledge and calls, not ownership. The actual part vector owns elements, and the caller owns Price. The focused trace explains the two dispatch steps that a class diagram alone cannot show.

focus.title: The element supplies its exact type
focus.what: This member bridges a base-class traversal to a concrete-type visitor overload.
focus.where: Virtual dispatch selects it when the actual Part object is Bolts.
focus.why: Inside this member, the compiler knows the element is Bolts.
focus.invariant: The visitor receives a read-only reference to the original element.
focus.risk: A direct visit(Part&) cannot select the concrete overload merely from runtime type.

focus.title: The visitor owns the type-specific operation
focus.what: This member prices a quantity measured as a count of bolts.
focus.where: The selected Bolts overload runs on the actual Price visitor.
focus.why: Pricing stays outside Bolts, allowing another visitor to report labels or other results.
focus.invariant: A bolt count is valid before multiplication and add checks the total limit.
focus.risk: Confusing counts and metres gives the wrong units even if all C++ types compile.

The comment states the unit-specific pricing task.
Multiply the validated bolt count by five cents per bolt.

summary: Visitor makes new operations easier across a stable type set.
accept provides a concrete-type step before visit.
Overload resolution remains a compile-time choice.
Visitors need their own state and error invariants.
New element types require changes to every visitor.
Variant is an alternative for a closed set of value types.

exercises.prompt: Change the bolt rate to six cents and leave the cable rate unchanged. What should the mixed-order total become?
exercises.hint: The quantities remain three bolts and two metres.
exercises.answer: The total becomes 98 cents: three times six plus two times forty. Update the expected mixed-order check while retaining the independent total-limit test, which uses cable only.

exercises.prompt: Visit Bolts(2), Cable(1), and Bolts(0) with one fresh Price. Then visit Cable(1) again using the same visitor. List the total after each call.
exercises.hint: The visitor accumulates rather than replacing its result.
exercises.answer: The totals are 10, 50, 50, and 90. Zero quantity contributes zero; using the same visitor for the final call continues the existing report.

exercises.prompt: A developer adds void visit(const Part&) to Visitor and calls it directly from the mixed-list loop. Why does that fail to reproduce the element-specific operation automatically?
exercises.hint: The static argument type still determines which overload is chosen.
exercises.answer: The Part overload is selected from the Part expression. Virtual dispatch can choose an override of that signature, but cannot switch to a different Bolts or Cable signature. Keep the accept step or use another explicit type-selection mechanism.

exercises.prompt: New reports arrive weekly, while the two element kinds have stayed fixed for years. Choose Visitor or adding every report as a new Part virtual member.
exercises.hint: Choose which source files should change for each new report.
exercises.answer: Visitor is a reasonable fit: each report implements the known type cases without editing every element. It introduces a shared type list, so document that adding a new part kind affects all report visitors.

exercises.prompt: Add Labels producing bolts=3 and cable-m=2 in traversal order without editing any element type. What regression check proves pricing is unaffected?
exercises.hint: Reuse accept with a different Visitor implementation.
exercises.answer: Implement both visit overloads to append the unit-labeled strings. Check the ordered string vector and confirm the earlier Price still contains 95. The reference solution also checks an empty label report and a zero-bolt label.

exercises.prompt: Explain when std::variant and std::visit would be preferable to this hierarchy. Include a cost of the choice.
exercises.hint: Consider simple value data and a closed list of alternatives.
exercises.answer: A variant fits a small closed set of value records and can store them without separate heap objects. Its type list appears in the value type, so adding an alternative can affect many callers and visitors. A polymorphic hierarchy can be more flexible when elements have independent identity and richer lifetimes.

lab.task: Add a Labels visitor with an ordered vector of strings. Bolts emits bolts=<count>; Cable emits cable-m=<metres>. Do not change Part, Bolts, Cable, or Price. Keep all original checks and print the two labels after existing output.
checks: The sample parts produce exactly [bolts=3, cable-m=2].
A fresh Labels visitor has no lines.
lab.answer: The reference solution implements two new visitor overloads and reuses the unchanged accept traversal. It keeps labels as strings owned by the visitor, so no references to parts survive the call. A stream-writing visitor would also work if output lifetime and failure handling were specified.

glossary.definition: An operation object with a separate entry point for each supported element type.
The compiler choosing a same-name function from its parameter types.
Selecting behavior using both the actual element kind and actual operation kind.
A design that names all allowed element alternatives in one known interface or value type.

problem_title: Add operations across a stable set of types

attachment_alignment.epub_section: Visitor — operations outside stable element types, acceptance methods, concrete element dispatch, and use with collections.
attachment_alignment.intent: Add operations across stable element types without putting every report inside those classes. The design makes new operations easier, but each new element type requires every visitor to account for it.
attachment_alignment.mechanism: Each element accepts a visitor through a shared interface. Its concrete accept implementation passes itself to the visitor entry point for that precise element type. The visitor supplies the operation for every supported type. Selection depends on both the actual element and actual visitor, a mechanism called double dispatch. Traversal decides which element comes next; acceptance decides which type-specific operation runs.

roles.responsibility: Let a caller apply an operation through a common element interface.
Carry distinct data and forward acceptance using their exact concrete type.

roles.attached: Visitor with two named visit operations
roles.responsibility: Require a type-specific operation for each supported element kind.
Implement one complete operation across the element set and retain any needed result.
Traverse mixed elements and apply the visitor without type tests.

source_walkthrough: The supplied array contains ConcreteComponentA and ConcreteComponentB through Component pointers. ClientCode loops over that array and calls Accept(visitor). When A accepts, it calls VisitConcreteComponentA(this); B calls VisitConcreteComponentB(this). The selected visitor uses each concrete element’s own data-access operation. There is no cast or component-type switch in the traversal.

The client first supplies ConcreteVisitor1 and then ConcreteVisitor2 to that unchanged loop. Output pairs A and B with the first visitor, then pairs A and B with the second. These four combinations demonstrate that the operation depends on both participating concrete types. The elements themselves are reused; adding the second visitor does not require a second element hierarchy.
attachment_alignment.adaptation: The new example changes generic A and B into bolt quantities and cable lengths. Price computes a checked total instead of printing type names, while the Labels lab adds another operation. Distinct source names such as VisitConcreteComponentA become overloaded visit functions taking const references. Each accept method still supplies the exact concrete element type, so the dispatch mechanism is preserved. Unique pointers own the mixed parts; visitors borrow them. The example adds quantity checks, explicit units, and a price limit. It does not add a tree or graph: a small mixed vector is enough to teach the mechanism.
attachment_alignment.recognize: Follow part->accept(price) to the concrete part’s typed visit call, then the concrete visitor implementation. Look for an outside operation with type-specific entries, reached through each element’s acceptance method. A loop alone is not Visitor.

contrast.distinction: Iterator supplies a way to visit elements in a collection without exposing storage. Visitor supplies the operation performed on each concrete element. Either can be used without the other.
Composite organizes individual and grouped elements as a common structure. Visitor can apply an operation to that structure, but this vector example needs no parent-child tree.
Strategy selects an interchangeable algorithm for a contextual task. Visitor additionally coordinates dispatch across a known set of concrete element types, with an explicit operation for each.

teach.action: Ask students to add pricing, labels, and audit output directly to Bolts and Cable. Identify why each new report would edit stable element classes.
Make a two-by-two grid of element kinds and visitor kinds. Match the four printed combinations to the exact Accept and visit calls.
Trace Part to Bolts::accept, then its const Bolts reference to Price::visit. Separate compile-time overload choice from virtual dispatch during execution.
Add Labels through the lab without editing parts. Then describe every interface and visitor change needed for a new Paint element.

checks.question: Why can visitor.visit(part) not choose the Bolts overload from a Part reference?
checks.answer: C++ overload selection uses the expression’s static type. The concrete accept member supplies the precise Bolts type before the virtual visitor call.

checks.question: Why might ordinary virtual methods be better if new part types arrive every week?
checks.answer: Visitor requires a new type-specific entry and corresponding implementations across visitors. Ordinary virtual operations keep adding new types more local when the operation set stays stable.
